families.s: HSE active and passive fire-protection technical measures
families.t: active systems, passive systems, firewater, domino protection, media, reliability, inspection and emergency response
f: Active fire-protection systems can extinguish, control or provide exposure protection against process fires.
Water sprinklers and sprays are widely used for storage vessels, process plant, loading installations and warehouses.
Foam systems may be more suitable than water for low-flash-point liquid fires.
Passive fire protection can delay vessel or structural failure when active water supplies are inadequate.
Fire walls can limit fire spread and thermal radiation to adjacent equipment.
System selection should consider substance hazards, inventories, separation, firefighting access and response capability.
Active systems require reliable supplies, testing and maintenance to remain available in an emergency.
Firewater and foam run-off should be contained and addressed in emergency arrangements.

families.s: HSE alarms, trips and interlocks technical measures
families.t: alarm systems, protection systems, trips, interlocks, control-system integration, case studies, reliability and operator response
f: Alarms, trips and interlocks are treated as part of the wider control-systems technical measure.
Alarm systems should provide operators with timely information about abnormal plant conditions.
Trips and interlocks are protection systems intended to move plant toward a safer condition.
Protection functions should be distinguished from normal process-control functions.
Alarm and protection design should reflect foreseeable major-accident scenarios.
Operator response assumptions should be supported by clear procedures and training.
Testing and maintenance are needed so alarms, trips and interlocks remain effective.
Past major-accident case studies illustrate the consequences of inadequate alarm or protection arrangements.

families.s: HSE control-room design for major-hazard installations
families.t: structural resistance, blast, toxic ingress, fire, ventilation, ergonomics, emergency control and safe haven
f: Control-room design should address both structural protection and effective ergonomic operation.
The control room should remain suitable for maintaining plant control after foreseeable undesirable events where emergency plans require it.
Foreseeable threats include explosions, pressure bursts, toxic releases and several types of fire.
Structural design should consider credible overpressure and the vulnerability of windows, roof equipment and internal fixtures.
Laminated or polycarbonate glazing may reduce injury from blast-related glass failure.
Protection against toxic-gas ingress can require sealing and suitable ventilation arrangements.
Air intakes should be positioned or isolated so contaminated air is not drawn into the control room.
Panels, displays and controls should support reliable operation during normal and emergency conditions.

families.s: HSE process and safety-related control systems
families.t: monitoring, logging, operator information, automatic control, integrity, alarms, trips, interlocks and safety functions
f: Instrumented control systems can monitor, record and log plant status and process parameters.
Control systems provide operators with information about plant and process conditions.
They can provide controls that allow operators to change plant status.
Automatic process and sequence control may operate during start-up, normal operation, shutdown and disturbance.
Safety-related systems require an integrity appropriate to the risk-reduction duty they perform.
Alarm systems and protection systems should be designed as defined functions rather than informal additions.
Trips and interlocks should act when specified dangerous conditions are detected.
Control-system lifecycle activities should include specification, validation, testing, maintenance and management of change.

families.s: HSE corrosion and materials-selection technical measures
families.t: internal corrosion, external corrosion, localised attack, material selection, corrosion allowance, inspection, monitoring and lifecycle management
f: Corrosion is a major cause of plant and equipment breakdown in process industries.
Material selection should reflect the process fluids, operating conditions and credible degradation mechanisms.
Using completely corrosion-resistant materials may be impracticable, so known corrosion rates and thickness allowances may be used.
Localised corrosion can cause failure much sooner than uniform wall loss would predict.
External atmospheric corrosion is an important cause of loss of containment.
Corrosion risks should be addressed during both plant design and operating life.
Inspection and condition monitoring should target the degradation mechanisms that could threaten containment.
Plant changes should be reviewed for effects on material compatibility and corrosion.
